a13-part1-cod.answer: ERCOT's interconnection status reports list a projected commercial operation date of 2027-11-04 for Kilby1 Part 1 Small Block Simple Cycle, a 371 MW gas turbine project by Energy Forge One LLC in Reeves County.[1] The date is the same in the July 2026 report and the October 2026 report.[2][1] As of the October 2026 report, the project had completed its screening study and started its facilities study, but had no interconnection agreement.[1]

a12-battery-now.answer: In the latest ERCOT interconnection status report provided (October 2026, published 2026-11-02), the Kilby1 Part 2 Tier1 BESS battery storage project by Energy Forge One LLC is listed at 330 MW.[1] This is smaller than the June 2026 ERCOT report, which listed the same battery project at 560 MW.[2] In both reports, the battery project connects at the Solstice Substation in Reeves County and has a projected commercial operation date of 2028-01-21.[1] The Quantum Storage battery project at 321.75 MW is in Haskell County and connects at the unrelated Kilby Switching Station, so it is not part of Project Kilby.[1]

a14-first-power.answer: Chevron says first power delivery from Project Kilby is anticipated in 2028.[1] That timing is linked to Chevron's Final Investment Decision, which Chevron said in June 2026 was expected by the end of 2026, subject to other conditions.[1] In October 2026, Chevron's Daniel Droog said the investment decision could slip to 2027 because of a state moratorium on new data center permits, but that Kilby was still on track to produce its first electrons by 2028.[2] The ERCOT interconnection report lists the earliest Kilby1 gas block with a projected commercial operation date of 2027-11-04, and the larger blocks later.[3]

a11-substation.answer: In ERCOT's latest interconnection status report (October 2026), all four Energy Forge One LLC Kilby1 entries in Reeves County list the #60404 Solstice Substation 345 kV as their point of interconnection.[1] In the earlier May 2026 report, three of the Kilby1 parts already listed the Solstice Substation.[2] However, the May 2026 report listed Kilby1 Part 1 (Small Block Simple Cycle) at a different point: a double tap of the 345kV Parker (1436) to Benbrook (1873 & 1869) double-circuit line.[2] The "Kilby Station" and "Kilby Switching Station" entries in the same reports belong to the unrelated Quantum Solar and Quantum Storage projects in Haskell County, not Project Kilby.[1]

a15-fid-timing.answer: In its June 22, 2026 announcement, Chevron said its final investment decision (FID) on Kilby was expected by the end of 2026, subject to completing other necessary conditions.[1][2] National Grid's July 2026 coverage and the Frontier Grid analysis also put FID in 2026.[3][4] However, Semafor reported on 2026-10-01 that Chevron's vice president for power solutions, Daniel Droog, said the decision could be pushed to 2027 after Gov. Greg Abbott imposed a moratorium on new data center permits.[5] Even so, Droog said Kilby remained on track for first power by 2028.[5]

a16-co2e-updated.answer: In the TCEQ permit file at technical completeness, the proposed allowable greenhouse gas emissions for Project Kilby are 13,890,275.01 tons per year as CO2e.[1] That file covers the 46-turbine scope, which includes 29 Solar T130 turbines added in an update on December 22, 2025.[2] The same table lists CO2 alone at 13,871,124.49 tons per year.[1] For comparison, TCEQ's plain language summary of the original application, published before that update, listed a lower CO2 equivalent total of 11,564,704.59 tons per year.[3]

a17-co2e-pls.answer: The plain language summary for permit 181895 lists a CO2 equivalent total of 11,564,704.59 tons per year for all facilities at the Kilby site.[1] The same figure appears in the summary as filed in the application, published 2025-10-17, including the Spanish version.[2][3] The summary itself notes that its figures may change during technical review.[1] A later emissions summary table in the TCEQ permit file at technical completeness lists a higher value, 13,890,275.01 tons per year of GHG as CO2e.[4]

a20-filed-date.answer: Energy Forge One LLC submitted the air permit application for the Kilby plant to TCEQ on October 17, 2025.[1] TCEQ's pending permit list shows the same date, 10/17/2025, for the Kilby application (permit numbers 181895, GHGPSDTX260, PSDTX1684).[2][3] The application was later updated on December 22, 2025, when 29 Solar T130 simple-cycle turbines were added to the project scope.[4]

a19-water.answer: Chevron says the Kilby plant plans to use non-potable, brackish groundwater rather than freshwater for power plant operations.[1] Chevron also says it is working on ways to reuse produced water from oil and gas operations.[1] An analyst brief likewise describes closed-loop campus cooling and nonpotable or brackish sources as proposed, but notes that initial fill water, construction water and water rights still require confirmation.[2]

a21-public-meeting.answer: The TCEQ notice scheduled the public meeting on the Kilby permit application for Wednesday, June 10, 2026 at 7:00 PM.[1] The meeting location was the Reeves County Civic Center, 1500 S Cedar Street, Pecos, Texas 79772.[1] The meeting was to have two parts, an Informal Discussion Period and a Formal Comment Period, and the notice was issued on May 5, 2026.[1] The pages provided show only the announced schedule and do not confirm that the meeting actually took place as planned.[1]

a22-permit-number.answer: The state air quality permit number for the Kilby Power Plant is 181895, which Energy Forge One LLC applied for alongside federal permits PSDTX1684 (Prevention of Significant Deterioration) and GHGPSDTX260 (greenhouse gas).[1] The application was submitted to TCEQ on October 17, 2025.[1] The same three permit numbers appear on TCEQ's pending permit list, which showed the application as technically complete in the October 30, 2026 snapshot.[2]

a18-nox-controls.answer: NOx from the proposed natural gas turbines will be controlled by selective catalytic reduction (SCR).[1] In the application's BACT analysis for the simple-cycle turbines, dry low-NOx burners, which are built into the turbine design, are proposed for use together with SCR.[2] The same analysis rejected the EMx/SCONOx catalytic absorption system as technically infeasible for large turbines.[2] The SCR uses ammonia to convert NOx to water and nitrogen, and the ammonia injection is optimized to limit unreacted ammonia slip to a proposed 5 ppmvd at 15% O2 for the combined-cycle 7HA turbines.[3]

a26-technically-complete.answer: TCEQ's RBLC summary form for the Kilby Power Plant, dated April 10, 2026, gives an estimated PN2 and technically complete date of 4/15/2026.[1] The same form estimates a final issuance date of 10/15/2026.[1] TCEQ's pending permit list showed the application as administratively complete in an April 10, 2026 snapshot and as technically complete in an October 30, 2026 snapshot.[2][3]

a24-national-grid.answer: National Grid, through its National Grid Ventures arm, agreed to invest $1.75 billion in Joulent.[1] Joulent's own announcement calls it a strategic minority investment and does not give a percentage, but press reports say the money bought a 35% stake in the company.[2][3] Joulent announced the deal on July 1, 2026; it is developing Project Kilby through a 50-50 joint venture with Chevron.[1][3]

c01-battery-change.answer: In ERCOT's interconnection queue, the battery storage piece of Project Kilby is listed as "Kilby1 Part 2 Tier1 BESS" (INR 28INR0457), filed by Energy Forge One LLC in Reeves County.[1] In the June 2026 ERCOT status report (published 2026-07-01), its capacity was listed as 560 MW.[1] In the October 2026 report (published 2026-11-02), the same project was listed at 330 MW, so the battery portion shrank between the two reports.[2] Its other details stayed the same in both reports, including a projected commercial operation date of 2028-01-21 and a study phase of "SS Completed, FIS Started, No IA."[2][1]

a23-suppliers.answer: The permit file names two turbine makers for Project Kilby: GE, for its 7HA.02 units, and Solar, for its Titan 350 and Titan 130 units.[1] The October 2025 application listed 17 turbines: 2 GE 7HA.02 combined-cycle units, 3 GE 7HA.02 simple-cycle units and 12 Solar Titan 350 simple-cycle units.[2] An update on December 22, 2025 added 29 Solar Titan 130 simple-cycle turbines for 'early phase power', bringing the total to 46 turbines.[1] The technical review page lists these 29 added units only as "simple cycle turbines" and does not name their make.[3] The application says the turbine vendor provided exhaust emission data, but none of the pages name the supplier or describe any supply contract beyond these turbine models.[4]

a25-final-issuance-estimate.answer: In its RACT/BACT/LAER Clearinghouse summary form for the Kilby Power Plant, dated April 10, 2026, TCEQ listed an estimated final issuance date of 10/15/2026.[1] The same form estimated that the application would be technically complete by 4/15/2026.[1] A TCEQ pending permit list snapshot from 2026-10-30 still showed the Kilby application as "Technically Complete Application", not as an issued permit.[2]

c03-turbine-change.answer: The original application, dated October 2025, proposed 17 combustion turbines: 2 GE 7HA.02 combined-cycle turbines, 3 GE 7HA.02 simple-cycle turbines and 12 Solar Titan 350 simple-cycle turbines.[1] In an update to the application on December 22, 2025, 29 Solar T130 simple-cycle turbines were added to supply 'early phase power' to meet customer needs.[2] According to the update, these turbines would supply approximately 393 MW of early phase power and would have the same controls and outlet emission limits as the Solar T350 turbines.[3] After the update, the project scope listed 46 turbines: two combined-cycle and 44 simple-cycle units, with the 29 T130 turbines not intended to be onsite long-term.[2]

c04-permit-status.answer: The Kilby application (permits 181895, GHGPSDTX260 and PSDTX1684) is listed on TCEQ's pending permit list with a date of 10/17/2025, which matches the October 17, 2025 submission date in TCEQ's notice of receipt.[1][2] In a snapshot of the list taken on 2026-04-10, the application's status was shown as "Administrative Complete Application."[1] By a later snapshot taken on 2026-10-30, the status had changed to "Technically Complete Application."[3] A July 28, 2026 analyst brief also described the application as technically complete, but noted that this is not the same as final authorization.[4]

u01-turbine-cost.answer: The provided pages do not state what the GE Vernova turbines cost. They identify the turbine models (GE 7HA.02 units) and note that Engine No. 1's founder procured four gigawatts of GE Vernova turbines, but they give no purchase price. One press page links to a headline about a "$7B Texas power plant," but that is not a turbine cost.

c02-capacity-change.answer: The original application, dated October 2025, described the Kilby site's nominal power generation capacity as approximately 2,595 megawatts, with two combined-cycle and fifteen simple-cycle turbines.[1] In the December 22, 2025 response to TCEQ, the company restated the original turbines' total nominal net output as 2,476 MW at defined site conditions (59°F, 60% relative humidity, 2,850 feet elevation).[2] The same update added 29 simple-cycle turbines for early phase power, with a nominal net output of approximately 393 MW.[2] TCEQ's later review summary, dated April 10, 2026, describes 46 turbines with a nominal capacity of approximately 2,869 MW, and notes that the 29 Solar T130 turbines were added in the December 22, 2025 update.[3] Chevron's June 22, 2026 announcement gives a different figure, saying Kilby is expected to deliver approximately 2.67 gigawatts.[4]

u04-ppa-price.answer: The pages confirm a 20-year power purchase agreement between Energy Forge One LLC (Chevron) and Microsoft for about 2.67 GW, but none of them give the price per MWh Microsoft will pay. Chevron says only that the project is targeting mid-teen returns. The Frontier Grid brief models fuel price cases in $/MMBtu, which is a gas cost and not the PPA price, and it lists PPA terms among the items still unknown.

u02-epc-contractor.answer: The provided pages do not name the plant's EPC contractor. A Latitude Media article published 2026-07-10 says Joulent had not yet announced the EPC contractor for its Kilby project and was finalizing a contract with "a brand name." The TCEQ permit pages refer to an EPC contractor only in general terms, in describing the commissioning phase. A Frontier Grid brief (tier 4) describes equipment and EPC as "Advanced by company statement" but does not name a company.

c05-solar-fate.answer: The solar part of Project Kilby's ERCOT queue entries, listed as "Kilby1 Part 5 Solar" (INR 28INR0460), was cancelled.[1] ERCOT's July 2026 status report shows this 500 MW solar project in Reeves County with a cancel date of 2026-07-06.[1] In the October 2026 report, the remaining Energy Forge One LLC Kilby1 entries are gas turbine and battery storage projects, such as "Kilby1 Part 2 Tier1 BESS" and "Kilby1 Part 6 Large Block Combined Cycle"; no solar part is listed among them.[2] The "Quantum Solar" project in that report connects at a Kilby Station in Haskell County and is not part of Project Kilby.[2]

c06-part6-technology.answer: Yes, the technology code for Kilby1 Part 6 (INR 29INR0199) differs between the two ERCOT reports.[1][2] The August 2026 report, published 2026-09-01, listed its technology as CC (combined cycle).[1] The October 2026 report, published 2026-11-02, listed it as GT, even though the project name still says "Combined Cycle."[2] Other details for this entry stayed the same in both reports, including the 1056 MW capacity and the projected COD of 2029-07-19.[2][1]

u06-lcoe.answer: The provided pages do not give a levelized cost of electricity for the Kilby Power Plant. They include a carbon capture cost analysis (for example, an estimate of $194/ton of CO2 removed) and capacity figures (about 2.67 gigawatts), but no cost per unit of electricity generated.

u10-revenue.answer: The provided pages do not state how much annual revenue the Kilby plant will earn from Microsoft. They describe a 20-year power purchase agreement for about 2.67 gigawatts and say the project is 'targeting mid-teen returns,' but they give no revenue figure or power price.

u08-engine-no1-price.answer: None of the provided pages say what Chevron paid Engine No. 1, if anything, for its share of Project Kilby. The pages describe Kilby as a 50-50 joint venture between Chevron and Joulent, which was spun out of Engine No. 1. The only investment figure given is National Grid Ventures' $1.75 billion for a 35% stake in Joulent. That is a separate transaction, not a Chevron payment.

u05-acreage.answer: The provided pages do not state the acreage of the Kilby site. They give its location in Reeves County, about 20 miles south of Pecos, with driving directions. They also say the area map shows 3,000 feet from the site's property line. None of them gives a site size in acres.

u09-dc-contractor.answer: The provided pages do not name a general contractor for Microsoft's Pecos data center. They only discuss the EPC contractor for the Kilby power plant. Latitude Media (July 10, 2026) reported that Joulent had not yet announced that contractor but was finalizing a contract with "a brand name." A Frontier Grid brief says National Grid stated that EPC capacity is reserved. Neither source identifies a contractor for the data center itself.

u07-mercuria.answer: The provided pages do not mention a Pecos Power Plant built by Mercuria or any Texas Energy Fund loan. They cover only Project Kilby (Energy Forge One LLC, a Chevron subsidiary) near Pecos, Reeves County. Kilby's capacity appears as approximately 2,869 MW in the TCEQ permit file and approximately 2.67 gigawatts in Chevron's announcement, but that is a different project and should not be attributed to Mercuria.

u03-construction-cost.answer: None of the provided pages directly states a total construction cost for the Kilby power plant; the only figure is in the title of a related-article link on an Energy Capital HTX page, which refers to a "$7B" plant.[1] That $7B figure comes from a link title on a press page, not from a regulatory filing or company statement, so it should be treated as unconfirmed.[1] The TCEQ permit file has a cost of 11972 $Million, but that figure is not the plant's construction cost: it is the estimated cost of adding carbon capture, which the developer used to argue that carbon capture is not cost-effective.[2][3]

runs.label: Lens baseline
runs.note: 18 questions the lens pages suggest, before any change for them.

l03-startup-simple.answer: The provided pages do not state how long a simple-cycle startup may last under the draft permit. The December 22, 2025 deficiency response mentions startup and shutdown only in arguing that vendor emission guarantees do not apply during those periods, and it gives no duration limit. The draft permit's startup conditions are not among the pages provided.

l04-startup-combined.answer: The provided pages do not state a maximum startup duration for the combined-cycle turbines under the draft permit. Page P7 mentions a 60-minute limit, but it applies to transitional load operation (ramp rates above 32 MW per minute), not to startups. The 60-minute figure on P7 and P8 is only used in emission calculations for startup and shutdown events shorter than an hour.

l02-nox-combined.answer: The provided pages do not show the draft permit's NOx limit for the Kilby combined-cycle turbines. The BACT analysis table (P7, P8) lists the TCEQ Tier I BACT requirement for combined-cycle turbines as 2.0 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 24-hour average. That is a general agency benchmark, not the limit written into Project Kilby's draft permit. The 2 and 3 PPMVD values in the same table come from other projects' RBLC entries (Alaska Gasline, Lansing, Southwestern Public Service, C4GT), not from Project Kilby. P1 and P2 say only that the turbines will use selective catalytic reduction for NOx, and they give no concentration limit.

l01-nox-simple-7ha.answer: The proposed BACT NOx limit for the simple-cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines is 2.5 ppmvd@15% O2, compared with 2 ppmvd@15% O2 for the combined-cycle units.[1][2] The federal performance standard cited for these turbines changed between filings, though the BACT limit stayed the same.[2] The October 2025 application said the 7HA.02 turbines were subject to an NSPS Subpart KKKK NOx standard of 15 ppmvd@15% O2.[1] A later supplement in the permit file (published 2026-08-06) instead applies Subpart KKKKa, which sets a high-load NOx standard of 5 ppmvd@15% O2 when the turbines run above 70 percent of base load.[2] Both documents say the federal standard is above the 2.5 BACT limit, and compliance will be shown with a continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS), using selective catalytic reduction for NOx control.[2][3]

l05-sulfur-solar.answer: For the Solar T130 turbines, the TCEQ technical review limits the turbines to firing natural gas with an SO2 emission limit of 0.0034 lb/MMBtu, which it says equals a fuel sulfur content of 1.2 gr/100 scf.[1] The October 2025 application, written when the Solar T350 units were the only Solar turbines in the project, proposed a fuel sulfur BACT limit for the simple-cycle turbines of 5 gr/100 scf on an hourly basis and 1 gr/100 scf on an annual basis.[2][3] That 5 and 1 gr/100 scf limit matches TCEQ's Tier I BACT for pipeline quality natural gas, so the 1.2 gr/100 scf figure in the later technical review is not the same number as the application's annual 1 gr/100 scf limit.[1] The technical review page for the Solar T350 turbines says only that sulfur emissions are based on the sulfur content of the fuel supplied to the site, and it gives no number.[4]

l07-turbines-44-46.answer: The pages do not show a change from 44 to 46; the 44 figure counts only the simple-cycle turbines, which together with the two combined-cycle turbines make up the 46 turbines.[1] The original application, dated October 2025, proposed 17 combustion turbines: 2 GE 7HA.02 combined-cycle units, 3 GE 7HA.02 simple-cycle units and 12 Solar Titan 350 simple-cycle units.[2] The count grew because 29 Solar Titan 130 simple-cycle turbines were added in an update to the application on December 22, 2025.[1] Energy Forge One said these 29 turbines would supply early phase power to meet customer needs, and they are not intended to stay onsite long-term.[3][1]

l08-avo-frequency.answer: The draft permit's condition for piping, valves, pumps and compressors in contact with ammonia requires audio, olfactory and visual (AVO) leak checks at least once every 12-hour shift, with at least eight hours between checks.[1] The same sentence ends with the words "once every four hours," which appears to be leftover wording from a marked-up draft, so the text was still being edited.[1] Reviewer comments on that page show the company asked for daily checks or once per shift, and TCEQ agreed to once per 12-hour shift with a minimum of 8 hours between checks.[1] The company then proposed removing the eight-hour interval requirement, and the pages do not show how that request was resolved.[1]

l06-sulfur-ge.answer: A draft answer failed the page check, so it is not shown.

l09-stack-sampling.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, stack sampling must occur within 60 days after the turbine (CTG) or auxiliary boiler reaches its maximum operating rate, but no later than 180 days after initial start-up of the unit.[1][2] The TCEQ Executive Director may also require sampling at other times, and requests for more time go to the appropriate regional office.[1] The regional office must be notified at least 45 days before sampling.[1] In its original application, Energy Forge One proposed similar timing: performance testing within 180 days after startup, or on completion of the required stack sampling, whichever comes sooner.[3]

l10-sampling-notice.answer: The provided pages do not state how much advance notice the TCEQ regional office must get before stack sampling. The draft permit's special conditions (Permit Numbers 181895, PSDTX1684, and GHGPSDTX260) refer to 'the test notice specified in paragraph A,' but paragraph A, which would set the notice period, is not among the pages provided. The pages do cover related timing: sampling must occur within 60 days of reaching the maximum operating rate and no later than 180 days after initial start-up, and final sampling reports are due within 60 days after sampling is completed.

l11-leak-repair.answer: The draft permit does not set a fixed number of days for repairing a leak from the SF6 circuit breakers; it says action must be taken "as soon as practicable" after the leak is detected.[1] Plant personnel must take one or more listed actions, including locating and isolating the leak if necessary, or starting repair or replacement of the leaking component.[1] If an immediate repair is not possible, a leak collection or containment system may be used to control the leak until the repair or replacement is made.[1] Separately, the breakers must be guaranteed to leak no more than 0.5% by weight per year, and they must have an alarm that alerts the control room when pressure falls below normal.[1]

l14-nh3-change.answer: The provided pages do not show any ammonia emission limit for Project Kilby, or any change to one during draft permit negotiations. They only mention ammonia in passing: the draft permit's planned maintenance table lists NH3 emissions from turbine stacks and maintenance activities, and the application describes ammonia injection for the SCR systems. No ammonia limit values, revisions or negotiation correspondence appear.

l13-ramp-threshold.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions for Project Kilby, transitional load operations are defined as a combustion turbine ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute, with each event not to exceed 60 minutes.[1] This matches what Energy Forge One requested based on turbine manufacturer information, namely excluding emissions during transitional load operations above 32 MW per minute.[2] The 5 MW per minute threshold that appears in the file comes from other permits (the Entergy permits and GW Ranch) that were cited as precedents, not from Project Kilby's own condition.[2][1]

l15-wholly-owned.answer: In its June 22, 2026 announcement, Chevron described Energy Forge One LLC as a wholly owned subsidiary that had signed the power agreement with Microsoft.[1] The same release said Chevron and Engine No. 1 had been collaborating on the development, known as Project Kilby.[1] Press coverage described the project itself, rather than Energy Forge One, as a 50-50 joint venture between Joulent and Chevron.[2]

l16-joulent-share.answer: Joulent has formalized a 50% ownership interest in Kilby, which it describes as its first project.[1] Joulent says it formalized this stake in connection with a $1.75 billion strategic minority investment from National Grid, announced July 1, 2026.[1][2] Press coverage describes Project Kilby as a joint venture between Chevron and Joulent.[3] Chevron's own June 22, 2026 announcement does not mention Joulent; it names Energy Forge One LLC, a wholly owned Chevron subsidiary, as the party to the Microsoft agreement and says Chevron and Engine No. 1 collaborated on the project.[4]

l17-epc-contractor.answer: None of the provided pages name the EPC contractor selected to build Kilby. A Latitude Media article (P1, published 2026-07-10) says Joulent had not yet announced the EPC contractor and was finalizing a contract with "a brand name." A Frontier Grid brief (P8) reports that National Grid states EPC capacity is reserved. The TCEQ permit pages refer to the EPC contractor only generically.

l18-ppa-lds.answer: None of the provided pages state any liquidated damages in the Microsoft PPA for late commercial operation. The pages confirm a 20-year PPA and a first-power target of 2028. The Frontier Grid brief (tier 4) lists 'PPA conditions precedent, remedies and phase acceptance tests' as unknown. It also says liquidated-damages protections are not disclosed, though that remark is about turbine and equipment supply, not the PPA.

l12-nh3-slip.answer: The application proposes an ammonia (NH3) slip BACT limit of 5 ppmvd at 15% O2 for the simple-cycle GE 7HA and Solar T350 turbines.[1][2] The same proposed limit of 5 ppmvd at 15% O2 applies to the combined-cycle GE 7HA turbines.[3][4] That is tighter than the TCEQ Tier I BACT requirement of 7-10 ppmvd at 15% O2, which is met by controlling ammonia injection to minimize slip.[1] These are proposed limits from the BACT tables, and the tables do not mention the 29 Solar T130 turbines, which were added to the project in a December 22, 2025 update.[5]

runs.label: Lens v1
runs.note: Permit guided retrieval: the latest draft's matching conditions and redline comment pages.

l04-startup-combined.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, a planned startup for combined cycle operation may not exceed 70 minutes per startup.[1][2] By comparison, planned startups for simple cycle operation are limited to 60 minutes per startup, and planned shutdowns may not exceed 60 minutes per shutdown.[2]

l03-startup-simple.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, a planned startup for simple cycle operation may not exceed 60 minutes per startup.[1] For comparison, planned startups for combined cycle operation are capped at 70 minutes per startup.[1] A planned startup begins when fuel is introduced and a combustion flame is established and recorded by the plant's control system. It ends when the turbine is in Environmental Compliance Mode, ammonia injection is in service, and startup emissions have purged through the continuous emissions monitoring system.[2]

l02-nox-combined.answer: In the draft permit's special conditions, the two combined cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines (7HACC1 and 7HACC2) have a nitrogen oxide (NOx) limit of 2.0 ppmvd at 15% oxygen, measured as a 24-hour rolling average.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup, and shutdown (MSS) periods.[1] NOx emissions during transitional load operations, meaning a ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute for no more than 60 minutes per event, may also be excluded from the averaging-time limit if certain conditions are met.[2] The limit matches the BACT level proposed in the application, 2 ppmvd at 15% O2 for the combined-cycle 7HA turbines.[3]

l01-nox-simple-7ha.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, the three simple cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines (EPNs 7HASC1, 7HASC2 and 7HASC3) have a NOx limit of 2.5 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hour rolling average.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup and shutdown periods.[1] NOx emissions during transitional load operations, defined as a ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute for no more than 60 minutes per event, may also be excluded from the averaging limit if certain conditions are met.[2] The October 2025 application proposed the same 2.5 ppmvd@15%O2 BACT limit for simple cycle operation and noted it is below the federal NSPS Subpart KKKK standard of 15 ppmvd@15% O2.[3]

l05-sulfur-solar.answer: A draft answer failed the page check, so it is not shown.

l06-sulfur-ge.answer: The draft permit limits the GE 7HA.02 turbines (EPNs 7HACC1, 7HACC2, 7HASC1, 7HASC2, and 7HASC3) to pipeline-quality, sweet natural gas with no more than 0.5 grains of total sulfur per 100 dry standard cubic feet.[1] The same 0.5 gr S/100 dscf limit also applies to the Black Start Generators (EPNs BSGEN1 and BSGEN2).[1] The October 2025 application had proposed a looser BACT limit for the combined-cycle turbines: 5 gr/100 scf fuel sulfur on an hourly basis and 1 gr/100 scf on an annual basis.[2] In the draft permit, a 5.0 hourly and 1.0 12-month rolling limit appears only for the Auxiliary Boiler, not the GE turbines.[1]

l08-avo-frequency.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, audio, olfactory, and visual (AVO) checks for leaks from piping, valves, pumps, and compressors in contact with ammonia must be made at least once every 12-hour shift.[1] If a leak is found, plant personnel must act immediately, but no later than one hour after detection, by isolating the leak, starting repair or replacement, or using a leak collection/containment system.[1] The date and time of each inspection must be noted in the operator's log or equivalent, and the permit holder must keep records of AVO checks.[1][2] The application describes this as following the 28AVO Program from the June 2018 TCEQ Technical Guidance Package for Equipment Leak Fugitives.[3]

l09-stack-sampling.answer: Under the draft permit, stack sampling must occur within 60 days after a turbine or boiler reaches the maximum operating rate at which it will be operated, but no later than 180 days after initial start-up of the unit.[1] The TCEQ Executive Director may also require sampling at other times, and requests for more time go to the appropriate regional office.[1] Before sampling, the appropriate TCEQ Regional Office must be notified not less than 45 days in advance.[1] Separately, performance testing must occur within 180 days following startup or upon completion of the required stack sampling, whichever occurs first.[2]

l10-sampling-notice.answer: Under the draft special conditions for Project Kilby, the appropriate TCEQ Regional Office must be notified not less than 45 days prior to sampling.[1] The notice must include items such as the proposed date for a pretest meeting, the date sampling will occur, the name of the sampling firm, the equipment and method to be used, and any proposed deviations from standard procedures.[1] Separately, the regional office must be notified at least 30 days before any required relative accuracy test audit (RATA) of the continuous emissions monitors.[2]

l07-turbines-44-46.answer: A reviewer comment on the redlined draft permit says the turbine count was "Updated from 44 to 46" and lists what the 46 include: 2 combined-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, 3 simple-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, 12 Solar T350 units and 29 Solar T130 units.[1] The change was marked "Accepted", and the later draft special condition authorizes 46 natural gas fired combustion generators.[1][2] The comment gives this breakdown of units but does not say why 44 had been written before.[1] For context, the October 2025 application proposed 17 combustion turbines (2 combined-cycle and 3 simple-cycle GE 7HA.02 units plus 12 Solar Titan 350 units), and it did not list the 29 Solar Titan 130 units.[3][4]

l11-leak-repair.answer: Under the draft permit's rules for piping, valves, pumps and compressors in natural gas and diesel service, a leaking component must be repaired as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 days after the leak is found.[1] If the repair would require a unit shutdown, it may be delayed until the next scheduled shutdown, and the component must be tagged in the meantime.[1] For components in contact with ammonia, the rule is stricter: immediately, but no later than one hour after a leak is detected, staff must isolate it, start repair or replacement, or contain it.[2] For equipment containing greenhouse gases such as the SF6 circuit breakers, action is required as soon as practicable after a leak is detected, with no fixed number of days given.[3]

l15-wholly-owned.answer: In its June 22, 2026 announcement, Chevron described Energy Forge One LLC as a wholly owned subsidiary that had signed the agreement with Microsoft.[1] The same release said Chevron and Engine No. 1 had been collaborating on the development, known as Project Kilby.[1] Press coverage described the plant itself as being developed through a 50-50 joint venture between Joulent and Chevron, but Energy Forge One was still identified as a Chevron subsidiary.[2]

l16-joulent-share.answer: Joulent holds a 50% ownership interest in Kilby, which it describes as its first project; it formalized this interest alongside a strategic investment from National Grid announced on July 1, 2026.[1][2] Semafor likewise describes Project Kilby as a joint venture between Chevron and Joulent.[3] Joulent says it developed Kilby through ongoing collaboration with GE Vernova and Energy Forge, a subsidiary of Chevron Power Solutions.[1]

l18-ppa-lds.answer: The provided pages do not state any liquidated damages in the Microsoft power purchase agreement for late commercial operation. They confirm a 20-year PPA with Microsoft. The Frontier Grid brief lists 'PPA conditions precedent, remedies and phase acceptance tests' as unknown. It also says liquidated-damages protections are not disclosed, though that remark refers to turbine and equipment supply rather than the PPA.

l17-epc-contractor.answer: None of the provided pages name the EPC contractor selected for Kilby. A July 10, 2026 press article (P1) says Joulent hadn't yet announced the EPC contractor and was finalizing a contract with "a brand name." A July 28, 2026 analysis brief (P8) says only that National Grid states EPC capacity is reserved. The TCEQ permit pages (P2, P4) refer to an EPC contractor without naming one.

l12-nh3-slip.answer: The draft permit sets an ammonia (NH3) limit of 5.0 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hour rolling average for every turbine group: the combined-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, the simple-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, and the Solar T350 and T130 units.[1] During transitional load periods, the averaging time for the CO and NH3 limits becomes a rolling 24 hours.[2] This matches the October 2025 application, which proposed a BACT limit of 5 ppmvd at 15% O2 for both the simple-cycle and combined-cycle turbines, below the TCEQ Tier I BACT range of 7-10 ppmvd.[3][4] The permit requires an NH3 CEMS on the turbine stacks, or an approved alternative that calculates ammonia slip from NOx CEMS readings.[5][6]

l13-ramp-threshold.answer: In the draft permit's special conditions, transitional load operations are defined as a combustion turbine (CTG) ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute, with each event limited to no more than 60 minutes.[1] During these periods, NOx emissions may be excluded from the averaging-time concentration limit only if certain conditions are met. One condition is that the turbine ramp rate exceeds 32 MW/minute during at least one hour of the 3-hour or 24-hour period.[1] Emissions during transitional load operations still may not exceed the maintenance, startup and shutdown (MSS) hourly emission rates for that turbine in the maximum allowable emission rates table (MAERT).[1]

l14-nh3-change.answer: In the marked-up draft special conditions, the ammonia (NH3) limit for the turbines is 5.0 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hour rolling average, and a reviewer comment says a value was "Updated from 2.0 to 5.0 per Table 3-2 in the application," which TCEQ accepted.[1] The page does not say exactly which table row that comment is attached to, so it is an inference that it refers to the ammonia limit.[1] Energy Forge One also proposed excluding CO and NH3, in addition to NOx, during transitional load operations, and pointed to a permit TCEQ had previously issued for a different project, GW Ranch.[2] TCEQ responded with a revised edit that added a new part E, under which the averaging period for the CO and NH3 limits becomes rolling 24 hours during transitional load periods.[2][3]

l04-startup-combined.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, a planned startup for combined cycle operation may not exceed 70 minutes per startup.[1][2] For comparison, planned startups for simple cycle operation are limited to 60 minutes, and planned shutdowns are also capped at 60 minutes each.[2]

l03-startup-simple.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, a planned startup for simple cycle operation may not exceed 60 minutes per startup.[1] A planned startup begins when fuel is introduced and a combustion flame has been established in the turbine and recorded by the plant's control system.[2] It ends when the turbine is in Environmental Compliance Mode, ammonia injection is in service, and startup emissions have purged through the continuous emissions monitoring system.[2] By comparison, planned startups for combined cycle operation are allowed up to 70 minutes.[2][1]

l02-nox-combined.answer: In the draft permit's special conditions, the two combined cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines (7HACC1 and 7HACC2) have a nitrogen oxide (NOx) limit of 2.0 ppmvd at 15% oxygen, measured as a 24-hour rolling average.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup, and shutdown (MSS).[1] NOx emissions during transitional load operations, defined as a ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute and lasting no more than 60 minutes per event, may also be excluded from the averaging-time limit if certain conditions are met.[2] This matches the BACT limit proposed in the application, which was 2 ppmvd at 15% O2 for the combined-cycle 7HA turbines.[3]

l01-nox-simple-7ha.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, the three simple cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines (EPNs 7HASC1, 7HASC2, 7HASC3) have a NOx limit of 2.5 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hr rolling average.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup, and shutdown (MSS) periods.[1] NOx emissions during transitional load operations, meaning ramp rates above 32 MW per minute for no more than 60 minutes per event, may also be excluded if certain conditions are met.[2] The application had proposed the same 2.5 ppmvd@15%O2 BACT limit for these turbines, which is well below the federal NSPS Subpart KKKK standard of 15 ppmvd@15% O2.[3]

l05-sulfur-solar.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, fuel for the Solar Titan 350 and Titan 130 turbines may contain no more than 1.2 grains of total sulfur per 100 dry standard cubic feet.[1] The fuel must be pipeline-quality, sweet natural gas.[1] The natural gas must be sampled at least every 6 months for total sulfur, and fuel supplier test results may be used to meet this requirement.[1] The October 2025 application's BACT analysis for simple-cycle turbines proposed a different limit: 5 gr/100 scf on an hourly basis and 1 gr/100 scf on an annual basis.[2] The 1.2 gr limit in the later draft permit is the value that appears in the permit conditions.[1]

l06-sulfur-ge.answer: The draft permit limits the fuel for the GE 7HA.02 turbines (both the combined-cycle and simple-cycle units) to pipeline-quality, sweet natural gas with no more than 0.5 grains of total sulfur per 100 dry standard cubic feet.[1] The same 0.5 gr S/100 dscf limit also applies to the Black Start Generators.[1] This is stricter than the BACT limit proposed for the combined-cycle turbines in the October 2025 application, which was 5 gr/100 scf on an hourly basis and 1 gr/100 scf on an annual basis.[2] In the draft permit, the 5.0 hourly and 1.0 twelve-month limits apply to the Auxiliary Boiler instead.[1]

l08-avo-frequency.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, audio, olfactory, and visual (AVO) checks for leaks from piping, valves, pumps, and compressors in contact with ammonia must be made at least once every 12-hour shift.[1] If a leak is found, plant personnel must act immediately, but no later than one hour after detection, by isolating the leak, starting repair or replacement, or using a leak collection/containment system.[1] The date and time of each inspection must be noted in the operator's log or equivalent, and records of AVO checks must be kept as part of the permit's recordkeeping requirements.[1][2]

l09-stack-sampling.answer: A draft answer failed the page check, so it is not shown.

l10-sampling-notice.answer: Under the draft special conditions for Project Kilby's permits, the appropriate TCEQ Regional Office must be notified not less than 45 days before stack sampling.[1] The notice must include items such as the proposed pretest meeting date, the sampling date, the sampling firm, the equipment and methods to be used, any proposed deviations, and how worst-case emissions will be determined.[1] Separately, the regional office must be notified at least 30 days before any required relative accuracy test audit (RATA) of the continuous emissions monitors.[2]

l07-turbines-44-46.answer: In the redlined draft permit, the count of natural gas fired turbines was changed from 44 to 46, and the reviewer's comment explains the new total by listing the turbine groups it covers: 2 combined cycle 7HA.02, 3 simple cycle 7HA.02, 12 Solar T350 and 29 Solar T130.[1] The change was accepted, and the clean version of the draft permit authorizes 46 turbines.[1][2] The pages do not say why the earlier figure of 44 was used or what it left out.[1] For context, the application as filed in October 2025 proposed only 17 turbines and did not list any Solar Titan 130 units, while the draft permit adds 29 Titan 130 turbines.[3][4]

l11-leak-repair.answer: Under the draft special conditions for piping, valves, pumps and compressors, a leaking component found by visual inspection must be repaired as soon as practicable, but no later than 15 days after the leak is found.[1] If the repair would require a unit shutdown, it may wait until the next scheduled shutdown, but the component must be tagged, and TCEQ may require an earlier shutdown based on the number and severity of tagged leaks.[1] For equipment in contact with ammonia, the rule is stricter: immediately, but no later than one hour after detecting a leak, personnel must isolate it, start repair or replacement, or use a leak collection/containment system.[2] For leaks from equipment containing greenhouse gases, such as the SF6 circuit breakers, the draft permit requires action as soon as practicable after the leak is detected and sets no fixed deadline.[3]

l13-ramp-threshold.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, transitional load operations are defined as a combustion turbine (CTG) ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute, with each event not to exceed 60 minutes.[1] NOx emissions during these periods may be excluded from the averaging-time concentration limit only if the qualifying concentration occurs in a 3-hour or 24-hour period where the ramp rate exceeds 32 MW/minute for at least one hour, and the emissions stay within the MSS hourly emission rates in the MAERT.[1] During transitional load periods, the averaging time for the CO and NH3 concentration limits becomes rolling 24 hours.[1]

l15-wholly-owned.answer: In its June 22, 2026 announcement, Chevron described Energy Forge One LLC as a wholly owned subsidiary of Chevron.[1] The same release said Chevron and Engine No. 1 had been collaborating on the development, known as Project Kilby.[1] Press coverage described the project itself as a 50-50 joint venture between Joulent and Chevron, while still calling Energy Forge One a Chevron subsidiary.[2]

l16-joulent-share.answer: Joulent has formalized a 50% ownership interest in Kilby, which it describes as its first project.[1] Joulent formalized this stake in connection with a $1.75 billion strategic minority investment in the company by National Grid, announced on July 1, 2026.[1][2] Press coverage describes Project Kilby as a joint venture between Chevron and Joulent.[3]

l12-nh3-slip.answer: The draft permit limits ammonia (NH3) to 5.0 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hr rolling average for every turbine group: the combined-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, the simple-cycle GE 7HA.02 units, the Solar T350 units and the Solar T130 units.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup and shutdown, and during transitional load periods the averaging time for NH3 becomes rolling 24 hours.[1][2] The October 2025 application had proposed the same BACT limit of 5 ppmvd at 15% O2 for both the simple-cycle 7HA and T350 turbines and the combined-cycle 7HA turbines, below the TCEQ Tier I BACT range of 7-10 ppmvd.[3][4] Compliance is tracked with an NH3 continuous emissions monitoring system, although the permit also allows approved alternatives such as calculating slip from NOx CEMS readings.[5][6]

l18-ppa-lds.answer: The provided pages do not state any liquidated damages in the Microsoft power purchase agreement for late commercial operation. They confirm a 20-year PPA and list remedies and liquidated-damages protections among items that are not public or are unknown, but they give no terms.

l14-nh3-change.answer: In the marked-up draft special conditions, a comment notes a limit was "updated from 2.0 to 5.0 per Table 3-2 in the application," and TCEQ replied that the change was accepted, though the comment text itself does not name the pollutant.[1] The resulting table sets ammonia (NH3) at 5.0 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hour rolling average for the combined cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines, as well as for the simple cycle GE and Solar turbines.[1][2] Energy Forge One also proposed excluding CO and NH3, not just NOx, during rapid load changes, citing ramp-related ammonia slip and a previously issued TCEQ permit for a different project (GW Ranch).[3] TCEQ responded with a revised edit and added a new part E, which makes the averaging period for the CO and NH3 limits rolling 24 hours during transitional load periods.[3][4]

l17-epc-contractor.answer: None of the provided pages names the EPC contractor for Kilby. A Latitude Media article published 2026-07-10 says Joulent had not yet announced the contractor and was finalizing a contract with an unnamed "brand name" firm. A Frontier Grid brief dated 2026-07-28 reports National Grid's statement that EPC capacity is reserved, but it does not identify the firm. The TCEQ permit pages refer only to "the EPC contractor" without naming it.

lh05-rata-notice.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions for Project Kilby, the appropriate TCEQ Regional Office must be notified at least 30 days before any required relative accuracy test audit (RATA).[1] The stated purpose of this notice is to give the Regional Office the chance to observe the testing.[1]

lh03-shutdown.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, a planned shutdown may not last more than 60 minutes per shutdown.[1] A planned shutdown starts when signals show the combustion turbine is no longer in Environmental Compliance Mode and ammonia injection is no longer in service for an intended shutdown, and it ends when a signal is received that the turbine has flamed out.[1]

lh06-heat-rate.answer: None of the provided pages state a heat rate guarantee from GE Vernova or describe the terms of its turbine supply agreement. The Frontier Grid brief (P5) notes that public disclosures do not cover 'guaranteed performance' for the GE Vernova turbines.

lh04-gas-sampling.answer: Under the draft permit's special conditions, the natural gas must be sampled at least every 6 months to determine its total sulfur and net heating value.[1] Test results from the fuel supplier may be used to satisfy this requirement.[1] Separately, for the initial compliance testing, fuel sampling using the methods of 40 CFR § 60.4415a may be conducted instead of stack sampling for SO2, with compliance based on 100 percent conversion of fuel sulfur to SO2.[2]

lh01-co-simple-7ha.answer: The draft permit's special conditions limit carbon monoxide (CO) from the three simple cycle GE 7HA.02 turbines (EPNs 7HASC1, 7HASC2 and 7HASC3) to 3.5 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hr rolling average.[1] This concentration limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup and shutdown (MSS).[1] During transitional load periods, the averaging time for the CO limit becomes a rolling 24 hours.[2]

lh02-nox-t130.answer: Under the draft permit's Special Condition 6, the 29 Solar Titan 130 turbines (EPNs T130SC1 through T130SC29), which run in simple cycle mode, have a NOx limit of 2.7 ppmvd at 15% O2 on a 3-hour rolling average.[1] This limit does not apply during planned maintenance, startup and shutdown (MSS) periods.[1] NOx emissions during transitional load operations, meaning a ramp rate greater than 32 MW per minute for no more than 60 minutes per event, may also be excluded from the averaging limit if certain conditions are met.[2] The October 2025 application as filed listed only 17 turbines and did not include the Titan 130 units; they appear in the later technically complete permit file.[3][1]
